https://abcnews.com/International/wireSt.text: Poland warns Russia likely to intensify provocations against European countries Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned of potential intensified Russian provocations at Ukraine's border crossings with Europe By CLAUDIA CIOBANU Associated Press and STEPHEN MCGRATH Associated Press September 11, 2026, 8:08 AM 1:50 FILE - Polish presidential candidate Donald Tusk, center, looks on during a ceremony for the 66th anniversary of the World War II battle of Kock in Wola Gulawska, Poland, Sunday, Oct. 2, 2005. (AP Photo/Czarek Sokolowski, File) The Associated Press WARSAW, Poland -- Two incidents along Ukraine's borders with Poland and Moldova this week are a preview of potential intensified Russian provocations at Ukraine's border crossing points with Europe, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said. Two people died when Russian drones hit the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova on Tuesday night while a “direct threat” to a Polish-Ukrainian crossing point on Wednesday night was only avoided thanks to cooperation between Warsaw and Kyiv, Tusk said on Thursday. He gave no further details of the incident, nor did he present evidence of Russian involvement. Tusk said he received a briefing on Thursday from CIA Director Jim Ratcliffe, who was recently in Moscow, about the risks posed by Russia in the region in the coming months. “Russia already decided to engage in provocative attacks on border crossing points, for example in Moldova,” he said, speaking on Thursday in Bratislava, Slovakia, during a meeting of central European countries and Ireland. “We expect similar actions regarding border crossings with Ukraine in other countries as well, including Poland.” Tusk added that he received information from Ratcliffe indicating Poland and Europe should be prepared for “various scenarios” on the Russian-Ukrainian front and in the countries on the European Union’s eastern flank. Ukraine shares borders with Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, and Moldova, as well as Russia and its ally Belarus. In recent weeks, Moldova, a former Soviet republic and a candidate for European Union membership since 2022, has been affected by multiple incidents near its southern border crossings with Ukraine. On Aug. 20, an explosion in a parking lot on Ukrainian territory, about 150 meters (490 feet) from Moldova’s southern Giurgiulesti border crossing, resulted in a vegetation fire that spread about 100 square meters (1,076 square feet) onto Moldovan territory. The same day, border police spotted a crater on Moldovan territory about 1 kilometer (0.62 miles) from the border, where they found debris from a type of drone used by Russia in Ukraine. A day later, Moldova’s Mirnoe border was temporarily closed after Russian strikes nearby on Ukraine. On Aug. 25, Moldova also suspended activity at its Vulcanesti border crossing after an Iranian-made Shahed drone struck the Ukrainian side. Moldova’s border police urged citizens “who hear drone noises or explosions” to remain calm and take shelter. After the border incident on Tuesday night at the Starokozache crossing, Moldova’s pro-Western President Maia Sandu condemned Russia, and said Moscow’s “brutal war is reaching our border.” “To deny the danger while Russian drones and missiles sow death and put Moldova in danger, and to criticize your country’s efforts to strengthen its defense system, is to choose betrayal over the safety of your own people,” she said in a post on Facebook. NATO chief calls for calm as intel agency warns Russia may ramp up hybrid attacks 1 day ago Iran live updates: Major atmosphere of mistrust,' Iranian president tells journalists 16 hours ago NATO jets scrambled in Poland, Romania as Russia strikes Ukraine Sep 23 Last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a border crossing with NATO-member Romania, in the east of the country along the Danube River, was “deliberately damaged, ... as well as export infrastructure.” Moscow has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's river ports throughout the war. Romania has also reported an almost threefold increase in drone incursions so far this year compared to the whole of 2025, and more than double the number of drones and drone debris found on its territory. Tusk has been warning for weeks that Russia could carry out a limited military or more significant hybrid provocation against Poland or the three Baltic countries, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, in the near future. “In the last few hours, I received a fairly detailed report directly from the CIA director regarding possible incidents in the coming months—and this is exactly what I’ve been saying and warning about for many months now,” Tusk said in Bratislava. In late August, Ratcliffe visited Moscow and held talks with his Russian intelligence counterparts, with Polish politicians speculating that one of the topics could have been the possible Russian threat to NATO. On Tuesday, Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland's minister overseeing intelligence services met with Ratcliffe at CIA headquarters in Virginia to discuss Poland's security and cooperation with the Americans. On Thursday and Friday this week, an American delegation including William Cappelletti Jr. from the Department of Defense and Thomas DiNanno from the Department of State, is visiting Poland to check out several potential locations for a permanent U.S. military base there. Poland has for years sought to host a permanent U.S. base as a strong guarantee of its security in the face of the rising Russian threat. Poland’s high defense spending and major U.S. arms purchases have persuaded the Donald Trump administration to consider putting a permanent base in Poland even as it reorganizes and reduces its overall military presence in Europe. ——— McGrath reported from Leamington Spa, England. https://bnn-news.com/bnn-in-focus/bnn-in.text: Photo: Magnific Advertisements One of the hottest issues this week is the plan by certain political forces to ban the transit of grain originating from Russia and Belarus through Latvia, despite the fact that the European Union has not sanctioned such cargo. Meanwhile, the industry warns that such a decision could have long-lasting negative consequences and could also put Latvia’s reputation as a stable and predictable transit corridor at risk. What would a grain transit ban actually mean for Latvia? BNN asked political scientist and co-owner of Mediju tilts Filips Rajevskis. “Shutting everything down is the easiest thing to do. I will repeat what I said when there was talk about dismantling the railway tracks. If we close our ports and tear up the railway, then perhaps, just to make things even safer and ensure everything is destroyed, we should burn down the entire country. Then no one will really need it. We will all be able to feel safe because if there is scorched earth all around us, no one will come here,” the political scientist says sarcastically. “The same applies here. Everything involves its own risks, concerns and situations that need to be dealt with intelligently, rather than politicising everything.” “I tend to believe that sanctioned companies are not operating in Latvian ports. The companies operating in Latvian ports are international traders, and many of the major traders are US companies.” Advertisements The political scientist also stresses that it would be very interesting to name the specific major international companies involved in transporting this grain through Latvian ports. Knowing which companies are involved would most likely also reveal how much Latvia could have to pay for failing to meet its obligations. “If contracts have already been signed, this business does not work like a small shop where you walk in and buy a carton of milk. These are long-term deals, and they certainly include penalties. So first we need to understand which companies are involved and who owns the grain. Then we can understand how much stopping grain transit would cost us. We can choose not to transport it, but we may also have to pay for terminating this business. These are risks that come at a cost.” Filips Rajevskis explains that if the issue is being discussed so loudly at the political level, taxpayers have the right to know the cost of every decision. “I am not saying that we should not stop it. I also believe that we should not support Russia or Russian exports. But we should not pointlessly end up in a situation where we are not helping Ukrainians while at the same time hurting ourselves.” Advertisements Asked by BNN about the possibility that unilateral decisions by Latvia could also affect grain shipments from Central Asia, including Kazakhstan, the political scientist urges looking at transit as a whole. “We can see how successfully cargo volumes are growing at the Port of Klaipėda, while ours are chronically declining. So the question is: what are these cargoes of some cosmic origin that the Lithuanians are handling at the Port of Klaipėda? This question should not be underestimated.” Filips Rajevskis stresses that it is also necessary to consider why all of this is happening. “The Black Sea and the Caspian Sea are closed to grain. Yet Ukrainians are also exporting grain. So the question is whether all these decision-makers have agreed that Ukrainian grain should be transported through Latvia. I would be very pleased if there were deals with Ukrainians and we could help them in their fight by transporting and exporting their grain. That is business too.” Advertisements Asked how he assesses the initiative by the Progressives and other parties to ban grain transit through Latvia, and whether this rhetoric is linked to the election campaign, the political scientist is critical: “If we are talking about all of this as pre-election rhetoric, I want to say that a campaign is being built on the back of the war. As cynical as it may sound, our politicians are campaigning on the war and people’s fear of war. And that is somewhat disturbing.” Share : Read also Editor's pick BNN in Focus Political scientist’s view: “Where will we make the cuts?” – Rajevskis warns of the cost of banning grain transit BNN in Focus Don’t stay at home – vote! https://www.delfi.lt/en/business/new-inv.text: Delfi EN Delfi Business 2026.10.09 10:03 New INVL fund of up to EUR 200mn will invest in Central and Eastern European banks Source: ELTA „Invalda INVL“ PHOTO: Įmonės nuotr. Follow Delfi on Google INVL, a leading alternative asset manager in the Baltics, has established the INVL European Banking Opportunities Fund, a fund of up to EUR 200 million that will invest in the capital of banks in Central and Eastern Europe. The fund’s investment geography will cover European Union member states and candidate countries, Invalda INVL said in a press release. The rules of the closed-end fund for informed investors were approved by the Bank of Lithuania on 8 October. The fund will be able to invest in both controlling and minority stakes in banks, as well as participate in capital increases. „The economies and banking sector of Central and Eastern Europe are growing faster than in Western Europe, but they still lack capital. We see opportunities to invest on attractive terms where we can contribute to the growth of banks as a long-term shareholder,“ says Vytautas Plunksnis, Head of Private Equity at INVL. The minimum investment in the fund is EUR 0.5 million, with a planned maximum fund size of up to EUR 200 million. The planned term of the fund is 6 years, with an option to extend for a further 4 years. The fund’s investment units are being distributed by the brokerage firm INVL Financial Advisors, which operates under the brand name INVL Šeimos biuras in Lithuania, and as INVL Family Office in Latvia and Estonia. „Transactions of this type in private equity are usually undertaken by institutional investors. This fund is a rare opportunity for private investors to invest alongside them,“ says Asta Jovaišienė, Head of the INVL Family Office. According to her, an investment in the fund is intended for investors who can tolerate higher risk. Due to the higher-than-usual minimum investment threshold, the fund is aimed at those who are able and willing to participate directly in large private equity transactions. The first fundraising stage of the fund is intended to be completed by the end of 2026. The Invalda INVL group has been active in the financial sector for more than three decades. Invalda INVL, together with an INVL fund, holds more than 14% of the shares in maib, the largest bank in Moldova. Along with consortium partners – the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and Horizon Capital – the combined stake is over 38%. Invalda INVL is also the largest shareholder in Artea, a bank operating in Lithuania, holding a stake of nearly 20%. These investments are characterised by long-term value creation. From 2018, when a consortium of investors became the largest shareholder of maib, until the end of 2025, the bank’s assets grew more than threefold, while its loan portfolio grew 3.6-fold. Meanwhile, from Invalda INVL’s entry as a shareholder in 2015 until the end of 2025, the assets of Artea bank (formerly Šiaulių bankas) increased 3.7-fold and its loan portfolio 4.8-fold. The group also includes a company providing family office services in Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, as well as a pension fund management company in Latvia. Previously, the group also managed other financial companies – the investment bank Finasta with its group of the same name, and an insurance brokerage business, all of which it profitably sold. Photograph: Thibault Camus/AP View image in fullscreen A protester throws a projectile towards police after a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday. Photograph: Thibault Camus/AP France Macron’s ‘vandals pay’ bill puts right to protest at risk Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponents Angelique Chrisafis in Paris Sun 25 Oct 2026 19.57 GMT Last modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 19.59 GMT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Emmanuel Macron has been accused by trade unions of trying to curb the fundamental French right to protest as the government fast-tracks a bill to make protesters pay for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves. The French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month of protests in which high-school students have blockaded schools demanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform. Trade unions and gilets jaunes (yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joining sustained street demonstrations in a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of its worst days of violence in years earlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings. The senate will this week debate the government’s proposed “vandals pay” law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests. Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing Read more The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the bill, which was originally prepared in the wake of violent clashes after Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the football Champions League in May, was “absolutely essential” after looting and burning during recent demonstrations across France. The bill comes as the government struggles to contain the current crisis. Marine Le Pen , of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN), has seen her frontrunner status in next spring’s presidential election boosted as she seeks to reinforce her law-and-order credentials and back police. Le Pen, who has lodged an appeal to France’s highest court over her conviction for embezzlement of European parliament funds , launched her presidential campaign on Sunday at a rally in Orléans, promising to “bring back order to France”. The RN has claimed the “vandals pay” bill was originally its idea and Le Pen said she would ensure damage to property was paid for by rioters. Le Pen told a cheering crowd of more than 8,000 people at the rally: “Vandals will pay and if it takes their whole life to pay, then they will spend their whole life paying.” She said: “We are going to restore the rule of law. Who can claim that there is rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?” Éric Coquerel, from Jean-Luc Mélenchon ’s radical left La France Insoumise, said on Sunday that the “vandals pay” law “would mean the end of street demonstrations” in France because people would not want to take the risk of being held responsible and made to pay up to €10,000 for vandalism they had not committed. The Communist senator Fabien Gay told the parliamentary TV channel Public Sénat: “No demonstration could take place again in our country.” In an open letter to Le Monde , leftwing trade unions and France’s Human Rights League wrote: “This unfair law, which is a serious attack on the freedom to demonstrate, should be abandoned, or risk a major step back for the rule of law.” At this weekend’s protests there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres. Although Macron has not put in place a state of emergency, the government and local authorities have introduced limits on demonstrating, including bans on gatherings in front of schools and demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in some places and extended periods of police custody for the record number of people arrested. NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France game Read more At demonstrations this weekend, many said they had come out to defend the French right to protest in the street. Street protests in France, which are seen as a fundamental way for people to make themselves heard by a centralised state, have regularly been used to express criticism of changes to the law, from pension changes to same-sex marriage . Serge Slama, a professor of public law at Université Grenoble Alpes, told Telerama magazine: “Although a state of emergency has been ruled out [by Emmanuel Macron] at this point, we have seen a number of decrees bringing a wide restriction on public liberties.” He said this was “unprecedented” and would benefit the far right if they won elections next year, allowing them to put in place further crackdowns without changing the law. Lecornu will meet representatives of protesting high-schoolers on Monday as the government comes under pressure to respond to their demands with funding and school repairs in order to avoid further school blockades.
